What I do: Write down what the ontology is for, who it's for, what it is NOT for, and 15 questions it has to be able to answer
Why it comes here: Everything after this gets checked against those questions. It's three pages of writing, no code, and it's the best hour I'll spend on the whole thing
What exists at the end: A requirements doc, and 15 questions that later become my evaluation chapter
What goes wrong if I skip it: I build classes nobody needs, and at the end I can't prove the thing works

What I do: Go through all 42 columns and decide: reuse someone's term, or invent one. Then check three things that could each save weeks: the CosIng RDF on GitHub, DermO on BioPortal, and whether Wikidata knows our 1,463 brands
Why it comes here: If CosIng already exists as proper RDF, our whole ingredient layer arrives free and we cite them. Finding that out AFTER building it would hurt
What exists at the end: A 42-row table that goes straight into the thesis, and possibly a free ingredient layer
Who told me to do this: Both LOT and MOMo say reuse before you build
What goes wrong if I skip it: I reinvent 28,573 ingredient entries that already exist

What I do: Draw each module as a diagram first, then write the Turtle. core, product, evidence, user, plus the Lebanon file that pulls them together
Why it comes here: The four change at completely different speeds. Product data moves weekly, medical knowledge barely moves. And I can hand a dermatologist ONE small file instead of 12,629 rows
What exists at the end: The ontology, plus the diagrams my chapter needs anyway
Who told me to do this: MOMo. Hansanie & Silva did the same and explained why
What goes wrong if I skip it: One giant file nobody can review, reuse, or update in pieces

What I do: Build the long helper file (one row per ingredient mention, about 295,991 rows), write the YARRRML mapping, run Morph-KGC, load into GraphDB with each source in its own named box
Why it comes here: This is what decides whether this is a METHOD or just a script. A mapping file can be audited and cited. Named boxes mean I can reload one source without disturbing the rest
What exists at the end: About 1.8 million triples, plus a mapping file for the appendix
Who told me to do this: TOXIN used R2RML. Abesova used OntoRefine
What goes wrong if I skip it: An unauditable script, and no way to trace where a statement came from

Step: 5 Make it think, then check it
What I do: Switch on the reasoner-computed classes, run HermiT, write the SHACL shapes, run OOPS! and FOOPS!. But PREDICT the numbers first, then see what the reasoner actually gives
Why it comes here: Predicting and then checking is a real test. If SensitiveSafeProduct doesn't land near 9,537, something in the model is wrong and I want to know now, not later
What exists at the end: Evaluation numbers. Plus those 593 sensitive-skin products with allergens finally showing up as a proper contradiction instead of a note in a README
Who told me to do this: Abesova for the defined classes. OOPS! and FOOPS! for the rest
What goes wrong if I skip it: I publish an ontology whose computed classes were never checked against reality
